## The research question

Company filings carry **tone**. The hopeful pitch: a contextual reader extracts
more useful information than a word list.

The disciplined question is narrower:

> Does a richer filing-tone reader predict the drift **after the filing is
> public**, better than a simple lexicon, **once we respect the timestamp and
> pay costs**?

*Everything hinges on those last two conditions.*

## Prior evidence narrows the question

- Finance-specific dictionaries improve on generic word lists
  [@loughran_mcdonald_2011].
- Finance-adapted contextual models improve several sentiment-classification
  tasks [@araci_2019; @huang_wang_yang_2023].
- Filing-language changes have been associated with later firm outcomes and
  returns [@cohen_malloy_nguyen_2020].

**Unresolved here:** does a richer text score improve a feasible downstream
return-ranking decision relative to the simple finance baseline?

## The data (and the planted truth)

Reproducible **synthetic filings** (a stand-in for SEC EDGAR — runs offline, fixed seed).
Each filing has a latent tone, and two returns follow it:

- an **announcement** jump at the filing date — strongly tone-driven, and *untradeable*
  before the filing is public;
- a faint **post-filing drift** over the next 20 days — weakly tone-driven, and the only
  genuinely tradeable target.

The filing is dated **45 days after** the period it describes. That gap is the
central information-clock risk.

## Two readers of the text

- **Baseline** — a shallow Loughran–McDonald-style lexicon: net (positive − negative) hits.
  Cheap, transparent, hard to beat.
- **Candidate** — a richer contextual-reader proxy. The pipeline can call
  **FinBERT**, but the committed offline output uses a deterministic stand-in.

The candidate must improve on the baseline out of sample before its additional
complexity counts for anything.

## The leakage trap

Align tone to the **period-end** date and the return window swallows the announcement pop —
a move you could never have traded. Align to the **filing date** and you keep only the
honest, post-public drift.

![](../figures/01_leakage.png)

The same score and text produce roughly **five times the measured association**
under the inadmissible timestamp.

## Honest, time-aware evaluation

Evaluate out of sample (never shuffle time). Compare the **information coefficient** and a
top-minus-bottom **tercile spread**, net of a 10 bp cost.

![](../figures/02_finbert_vs_lexicon.png)

## The result

- Removing the timestamp leak cuts the apparent signal by **~5×**.
- On the honest target, the richer reader's edge is **small and does not clearly
  beat the lexicon**.
- The experiment does not provide enough uncertainty evidence to treat that
  small difference as stable.

**This is a good negative result** — the disciplined finding is that the easy "NLP alpha"
was mostly leakage.

## Limitations

- **Synthetic data** — the experiment does not estimate predictability in real
  SEC filings.
- **Offline proxy** — the committed run does not test FinBERT itself.
- **One universe, one horizon** — no sector/size controls, a single tercile cut.
- **Stylized 10 bp cost** — a filing-clustered strategy would likely pay more impact.
- **No multiple-testing accounting** — a real model/lexicon/horizon search needs a deflated
  Sharpe and a trial count.

## Takeaway

The question was never *"does the model sound fluent?"*

It is *"does its tone predict a return you could actually have traded, after costs?"*

Here — **barely.** And that answer, honestly arrived at, is the assignment.
